item.title: Five of the Main Challenges Awaiting Britain’s New Prime Minister
item.description:
It’s the biggest job in British politics, and Andy Burnham has had relatively little time to prepare. After he was installed in Downing Street as prime minister on Monday, Mr. Burnham now will need to make dozens of decisions each day, resolve disputes among ministers and act as the political figurehead of the government.

He faces a long and daunting list of issues facing 21st-century Britain. Here are some of the big ones.

After years of stagnating living standards dating back to the 2008 global financial crisis and made worse by Brexit and the Covid-19 pandemic, Mr. Burnham needs to introduce tangible improvements for Britons. He has vowed to stick to his party’s 2024 general election pledge not to increase the main taxes, however, and will face many of the same challenges as Keir Starmer, whom Mr. Burnham is replacing as prime minister. One key decision: who will be chancellor of the Exchequer.

With the war in Ukraine continuing and the conflict in the Middle East escalating, foreign policy will be an unavoidable priority even if Mr. Burnham might prefer to focus on domestic issues. So far, the indications are that Britain’s stance on the two conflicts is unlikely to change significantly, given that Jonathan Powell, who played a key role as Mr. Starmer’s national security adviser, is expected to remain in his job.

Mr. Starmer cultivated close ties with President Trump before enraging him by refusing to give his full-throated support for the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran. The United States remains Britain’s most important security partner, but Mr. Trump and his policies are deeply unpopular here. So the new prime minister will have to decide how to balance those considerations and how much energy to devote to cultivating a mercurial U.S. president.

Frustration over military spending levels prompted the resignation last month of Mr. Starmer’s defense secretary, John Healey, who argued that a proposed increase in the money destined for the military was insufficient. A few weeks later, Mr. Starmer announced plans to raise military spending by 15 billion pounds (about $20 billion) over the next four years. But he left the details of where that money would come from — and which departments might need to cut their budgets as a result — to Mr. Burnham.

Net migration to Britain has dropped sharply in recent years because of more restrictive policies introduced at the end of the previous Conservative government’s term in office, which the Labour Party has continued and extended.

However, opinion polling suggests that concern about immigration remains a top issue for many voters, and only a minority of people surveyed are aware that net migration has fallen.

In May, Mr. Burnham acknowledged that the “trend is significantly down,” but said that net migration “needs to fall further.” He has signaled that he will largely continue the tough policies of Mr. Starmer’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood. Her approach, including making it harder for legal migrants to gain permanent residency, has provoked opposition among some Labour lawmakers and progressive voters, so Mr. Burnham may try to find a compromise.

Britain’s welfare bill is rising. One reason is the growing number of claims from working-age people with mental health conditions, many of whom are young and unemployed. But the biggest chunk of Britain’s social security spending — more than half of the total — goes to retired people, through state pensions and other support. That spending has been pushed higher by an aging population and the so-called triple lock, which guarantees pensions increase by the highest of three measures.

Controlling those costs could free up resources for other policies, including Mr. Burnham’s plan to build more social housing. But Mr. Starmer’s efforts to curb welfare entitlements provoked a rebellion among Labour lawmakers that forced him to retreat, underscoring the political challenge of the task.

item.title: Aiming for My Fastest Marathon, I Turned to Distance Running’s Mecca
item.description:
From the moment the race started, my hamstrings began to ache — a dull throbbing that I knew could derail my run.

Just hours earlier, I had woken to an overcast May morning feeling excited to run the Cape Town Marathon. My lungs were strong, and my legs felt lighter than they had before any of my 15 previous marathons. My goal seemed possible: to run the race in 2 hours 50 minutes, more than seven minutes faster than the personal best I had achieved 14 years earlier, at 29.

My attempts to better that time over the years were mostly derailed by leg cramps. No gel, electrolyte drink, potato or salt packet could prevent those crippling moments in races, when it felt like someone was playing tug of war with my hamstrings.

As I reached my 40s, though, I began doing the little things that my younger, more athletic self ignored. I strength trained, foam rolled and stretched more frequently. I gave my muscles more time to recover. I slept more. I ran faster than I expected.

But I had cramped throughout the final 13 miles of the last marathon I raced, in November. I didn’t know how else I could improve at that point. A friend suggested training in Iten, a Kenyan village in the Great Rift Valley, which has produced some of the best marathoners in the world. I spent a week running there in April.

Now as the niggling in my hamstrings so early in the race began to worry me, I thought back on that training. If I wanted to hit my target, I would need to channel the skill I had not known was so crucial to those runners’ success: their mind-set.

On my first morning in Iten, I stood along the main road as packs of runners bounded past along the red dirt paths, like flocks of birds gliding in formation, their strides smooth, their posture straight. They moved with an envious efficiency. Almost every runner looked exceptionally fit.

This is a village where few people run recreationally. Most are hoping to win prize money in major competitions or, like the team I trained with, are trying to win scholarships to run college track in the United States.

“It’s running for their lives,” Richard Mukche, the team’s coach, told me of the ethos in Iten. Nearly 60 percent of the roughly half a million residents of Elgeyo Marakwet, the county that includes Iten, live in poverty.

About 30 years ago, Iten was a speck of a village with just a handful of rural homesteads and a handful of runners. After some of those early runners won international competitions, word spread about the benefits of training in Iten — the high altitude and the serenity — and it grew into a running mecca. It now serves as a base for Olympians and world champions from other countries, who spend weeks or months cloistered in camps that cater to their every training need. Amateur runners like me are a regular presence, helping to sustain the local economy — I paid about $700 for a week of training at a camp complete with meals and massages — as they try to improve their abilities by training with Kenyan runners.

Coach Richard is himself a Kenyan former elite athlete who trained in Iten and ran a 2:16 marathon in his day, which would still clock him in the top 20 finishers of last year’s New York City Marathon. He has been coaching for the past 16 years, mostly 20-somethings shooting for scholarships, but also world-class runners from abroad. Some of his athletes have competed in the Olympics and in major marathons. About six, including his daughter, have earned scholarships.

My first morning, when I joined the roughly 20 Kenyan runners currently under his wing, I was eager to run hard. Could I keep up with them?

But as I would come to learn, much of the training philosophy in Iten is about restraint, rather than excess. Coach Richard drilled in me an almost biblical commandment of Kenyan training: Listen to your body.

My first workout, he said, would be 5 miles at a relaxed pace — “Pole! Pole!” as they call easy runs in Swahili. He wanted my body to adjust to the altitude, which, at a mile and a half above sea level, is a half mile higher than where I live in Johannesburg.

So, I set off at a 8:30-per-mile pace, running past the not-so-subtle reminders of why Iten is a running destination. Past the arch over the main road that says welcome to the “Home Of Champions.” Past the “Champions Barber Shop” and “Champions Wines & Spirits.” By the end, I couldn’t help but feel optimistic — I hadn’t been bothered by the high altitude, which makes it harder to breathe but over time produces red blood cells that make breathing easier at lower elevations.

That evening, when I joined Coach Richard, his team and dozens of others at the Iten Sports Club to watch the Boston Marathon — local hero John Korir blazed his way to victory in course record time — I met Amanal Petros, Germany’s record-holder in the marathon, who was training in Iten for the London Marathon.

Petros has trained at other popular distance running hubs like Flagstaff, Ariz.; Boulder, Colo.; and St. Moritz, Switzerland. In those cities, he said, it takes months to find training partners on his level, while in Iten, he can find a dozen by just going to the main road in the morning.

“There’s nothing here. It’s just animals or runners,” he said. “You focus only on training, on your goal.”

For years after running in high school, I lost my motivation. The constant pursuit of faster times had made running feel like a chore. But then encouraged by a friend, I ran a marathon and then another. I broke three hours for the first and only time at the Chicago Marathon in 2012, clocking 2:57:32.

When I moved to Johannesburg five years ago, I was 38 and had pretty much resigned myself to the fact that my fastest days were behind me. But something changed. Living for the first time at a high altitude — nearly 5,600 feet — in a city with relentless hills, I became more fit than I had ever expected to be at my age.

In 2023, exactly six months before my 41st birthday, I won a half marathon in suburban St. Louis in my fastest time ever, bettering a mark I had set 11 years earlier. I felt like I was keeping mortality at bay. I wanted to see what my body could do.

And so, as day 2 of training in Iten began, I was excited to be able to push myself with the group. Coach Richard had us run 400-meter (one lap) repeats on the track. I felt great from the start, coming in a little over 80 seconds on each. I even talked Coach Richard into letting me do 15 laps, like some of the other runners, rather than the 10 he had assigned me. And when I was done, I wasn’t entirely drained.

“Who still has more energy?” Coach Richard asked us afterward. “In training, it’s better when you finish, you can still do something after. You don’t have to die completely.”

Paying attention to how I felt was the focus of much of my training in Iten. That simple question — how do you feel? — guides most runners in the area. It’s an approach that stands in stark contrast to the emphasis on technology and markers like VO₂ max and average heart rate promoted by most coaches and online influencers these days.

“Eat, sleep, run,” is how Coach Richard described the routine in Iten.

The simplicity is in some ways born out of circumstance. Most athletes here can’t afford the watches, carbon-plated super shoes or electrolyte gels that many privileged runners rely on. Some of the young people I trained with — people who were running at elite speeds — had holes in their shoes and drank water mixed with cheap glucose packets.

When athletes reach world-class levels in the United States and Europe, it’s common for them to follow individualized training plans. They often run alone or with just a few partners.

But there’s a pack mentality in Iten — runners generally run in big groups. In a crowd, a strenuous pace can feel comfortable; you’re syncing your strides with those around you and focusing on staying on the heels of the person ahead of you.

“Enjoy the rhythm, forget the pain,” is how Emmanuel Kipruto, an elite runner and coach in Iten, described group running.

The runners explained to me that the group also encourages discipline. You cannot sleep in when you know you need to meet your teammates in the morning to run. And there is competition within the group. When you see your teammates have success, it pushes you to try to keep up with them.

The ultimate group session in Iten takes place every Thursday when there is a fartlek workout, open to anyone who wants to participate. In fartlek trainings, runners alternate between fast, intense intervals and slow, relaxed ones as a way to build endurance and practice changing speeds.

The workout can attract hundreds of runners, from elites to amateurs. Dozens showed up the day I was there, and the regimen for the day was daunting: 13 repetitions of running one minute easy followed by three minutes hard.

By the end of the first 3-minute interval, I had slipped to the back of the pack. By the second, they had left me in their dust, literally — even the runner I saw hunched over vomiting during the first interval. I called it quits after 10 intervals. The pack was far out of sight, and each breath I took felt like someone was smothering me with a pillow.

It was humbling. The altitude I snickered at on previous days was now exacting its revenge. I felt like an amateur among pros, like a rec league baller trying to dunk on LeBron James.

Coach Richard said he saw progress, though. My body seemed strong, he told me, and that was important so that I could train the next day. I controlled my pace well, which is critical for racing, he said.

“I told you, listen to your body,” he said.

I had come to Iten hoping to find the secret to running success. What I was learning was that the secret was trusting how my body felt — understanding my own boundaries. It was OK to slow down if my body demanded it. But it was also fine to let loose.

Two days after the fartlek session, I prepared for my final run in Iten, nearly 16 miles along Moiben Road, a paved, relatively flat stretch where local runners do most of their long runs. Coach Richard told me to start my run at 75 percent effort, and pick it up if I felt good.

I was a bit uncertain as I set off alongside Vincent Cheruiyot, the team captain assigned to pace me. We settled into a nice rhythm faster than 7:15 per mile, a brisk but far from brutal pace. The running felt comfortable as I focused on the beautiful mountain vistas and watching the elite athletes blow past me, including the 10 kilometer world-record holder, Agnes Jebet Ngetich.

With about three miles to go, my body told me I could handle more. Our pace dipped below 7 minutes per mile. By the time we were on our last mile, the sweat was dripping, my hamstrings were taut, but I knew I could push the pace, matching Vincent next to me stride-for-stride. When we were done, my body felt bent but not broken, my lungs refreshed. Vincent and Coach Richard flashed wide smiles. I felt the progress.

As I prepared to leave Iten, I knew the workouts I had learned were sustainable. I hadn’t trained long enough to experience the full physical benefits, but running is as much a mental challenge as a physical one. I could sense that I had achieved a mental recalibration that I had not been expecting.

“Listen to your body.” That had been Coach Richard’s instruction, and hamstring troubles early in the Cape Town Marathon meant that my body needed me to be conservative. So I relaxed my pace, hoping that I would warm up and the discomfort would go away. By mile six, I felt better.

I was a little behind my goal pace, so I decided to open up my stride. Eleven of my next 13 mile splits came in under my target of 6:29 per mile. I was blowing past other runners and my lungs were at ease.

Then on mile 20, we hit a long, steady, sneaky hill. My pace slowed. I kept my focus straight ahead, and thought about the efficiency of the strides of the Kenyans I ran with in Iten. I tried to mimic that. I pushed, but my body didn’t have more to give. My watch said that 2:50 wasn’t going to happen. But I still could beat my personal best, I thought.

I grit my teeth through those final miles. The sun beat down. I started losing my breath. But I thought back to Iten, when the thin air had me gasping and the steep dirt paths had my legs straining, and I felt more than prepared for this moment. I thought about Emmanuel’s advice to “enjoy the rhythm, forget the pain.”

I saw the finish line and found one last surge.

I crossed in 2:53:50, smashing my previous record by nearly four minutes.

One thing that surprised me about Iten was how comfortable I felt among those elite runners even though I was not nearly as fast as them. The local elites there relish the chance to run with and get to know amateurs who visit from around the world. They don't care how fast you are. Really!

Part of the reason is that they can sometimes turn to visitors they've developed relationships with for material support. Many Kenyans training there come from very modest means and can't often afford expensive running watches or shoes. One young woman I met had gotten a scholarship offer in the U.S. but could not afford the roughly $200 she needed to get an appointment at the US consulate for a visa.

It's become part of the exchange in the Iten experience. They help to pace you and give you tips to make yourself a better runner. And in return, some runners will pay them tips, and sometimes down the line help with bigger asks they may have.

Edwin Okoth contributed reporting from Nairobi, Kenya.

item.title: In Venezuela’s Rubble, a Search for the Family Pets
item.description:
As Venezuela counts its dead, clears away collapsed buildings and begins its long recovery from last month’s devastating earthquakes, another consequence of the disaster has emerged: the pets left injured, orphaned or separated from their owners.

Volunteers are reuniting cats and dogs with families who may have lost relatives, homes and nearly everything else. Others are caring for pets with missing or deceased owners, or trying to help families who have no way to care for their animals.

“Everyone was focusing on rescues, but there are also people who managed to escape with their pets and don’t have the means to feed them,” said Nieves Peña, director of an animal rescue organization, Mi Primer Rescate.

In the coastal state of La Guaira, which was hardest hit by the quakes, “everything is closed, everything is destroyed,” Ms. Peña said. “There’s nowhere to buy dog food.”

Her organization, based in the city of Valencia, traveled to La Guaira the day after the June 24 earthquakes to treat injured animals, distribute pet food to displaced families and create a foster network while they searched for owners of pets.

Even as people who survived the disaster are coping with the trauma of losing loved ones and having no home, surviving pets also face challenges.

“There is a lot of stress on the animals,” Ms. Peña said. “Changes in weather and spaces can weaken their immune systems and bring about viral diseases.”

Dr. Ludeimar Rosendo, a veterinarian who traveled from the western city of Barquisimeto to volunteer at a makeshift clinic at a McDonald’s restaurant in La Guaira, said she had treated or performed surgeries on about 700 animals since the disaster, with 20 to 30 arriving every day.

Some reunions between owners and their pets came after days of uncertainty.

When the earthquakes struck, Osdalys Santana, her husband and teenage son were coming home from their food stand at Los Cocos beach in La Guaira. Their two younger children were at home on the eighth floor of an apartment building with the family’s two dogs, Luna and Canela.

Though the building collapsed, the two children were rescued, but the dogs were nowhere to be found. Ms. Santana worried about Luna, her 5-year-old pinscher mix who trembled at the sound of firecrackers and had never liked being outside. At home, she said, Luna was a pampered family pet who loved to sleep and cuddle, even climbing into a chair to eat at the family table.

She had no idea that rescuers had pulled Luna from the rubble.

While Ms. Santana was spending her days in a hospital in Caracas with her son, who had a fractured leg, Luna was treated by volunteers and placed with a foster family.

Ms. Santana posted photographs online, hoping someone had seen Luna. Eventually, someone recognized her.

“Ever since Luna came into our lives, she’s been like another daughter. We love her so much, with my children it’s something else entirely — it’s special,” she said. “Thank God, we are so happy to have her back.”

Canela remains missing.

“I have faith that at some point, I will find her and get her back,” said Ms. Santana.

While trained rescue dogs have played a crucial role in the search effort, one family’s pet in La Guaira may have also helped save a life.

When a 1-year-old dog named Toby escaped from the rubble of a building, he kept evading rescuers despite being injured, instead repeatedly running back to the same spot in the debris, according to building residents.

They searched there and discovered an 11-year-old boy, Kenger García, trapped beneath the collapsed building where he had survived for 78 hours, dehydrated and bruised but alive.

Toby was the García family’s dog.

Kenger’s aunt, María Sandoval, posted photos of Toby on social media until he was identified. Ms. Peña, the director of Mi Primer Rescate, returned the dog herself to Ms. Sandoval.

“Toby was truly the one who helped save his owner,” said Ms. Sandoval. “He is the reason that they suspected that someone was still alive amid all that rubble.”

For Andrea Villasana, 24, a physiotherapist who traveled from eastern Venezuela to La Guaira with a volunteer convoy delivering donations, one frightened puppy became a rare source of relief after days surrounded by devastation.

She found the dog darting through traffic and damaged buildings before other volunteers caught her. As they searched unsuccessfully for the dog’s owner, residents began stopping to pet her. One man insisted on giving her half of the arepa he was eating.

Later that evening, exhausted residents gathered around the dog, pulling out flashlights to see her and feeding her pieces of tuna and dog food.

“It really changed everyone’s expression. It’s like being all day waiting for good news or just wanting to see something that gives you a little bit of hope,” said Ms. Villasana. “They were smiling despite everything.”

item.title: Trump Says Netanyahu Will Not Be Arrested in the U.S.
item.description:
President Trump said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would not be arrested in the United States, “in any way, shape, or form,” saying Mr. Netanyahu was fighting the Islamic Republic of Iran and that Iranian leaders are the ones that should be arrested.

His comments, posted on social media, came after Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations on Monday fired back at New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who has said he is looking into whether he can arrest Mr. Netanyahu, when he visits the U.N. headquarters in September.

The “threat is empty,” the ambassador, Danny Danon, said in an address to the U.N. General Assembly. Mr. Danon said there is “no legal basis” for an arrest and he accused the mayor of engaging in “political theater” to excite his “radical base.”

When Mr. Mamdani was campaigning for mayor, he had pledged to arrest Mr. Netanyahu on his annual visit to the U.N. General Assembly this September. It would be based on an International Criminal Court warrant citing alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in connection with the war in Gaza, following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.

That warrant was issued in 2024. Mr. Netanyahu and Israel’s former defense minister, Yoav Gallant, were accused of having “intentionally and knowingly deprived” Gaza’s population of food, water, fuel and medicine, which they have denied.

In an interview with The New York Times published on Saturday, Mr. Mamdani said he was in “an active conversation” with the city’s Law Department on whether he had the authority to arrest the Israeli leader while he was visiting the U.N.

“Whatever the law allows me to do in New York City, that’s what we will do, but we won’t be writing our own laws to that end,” he said.

Both Israeli and American officials, however, have rejected Mr. Mamdani’s effort, and even some vociferous critics of Israel have suggested that an attempted arrest of Mr. Netanyahu in New York could be problematic.

Mr. Danon has insisted that Mr. Mamdani has no authority to pursue such an arrest, noting that the United States is not a party to the Rome Statute, which created the I.C.C. He said that Washington does not recognize the jurisdiction of the court, among other obstacles.

Indeed, the Trump administration is looking to systematically dismantle the court, which investigates some of the gravest crimes in the world.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in The Wall Street Journal last week that the U.S. seeks to prevent “a world in which U.S. soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders could be dragged before an international court.”

In Mr. Danon’s address on Monday, he also cited the U.N. Headquarters Agreement of 1947 as protecting Mr. Netanyahu and other world leaders who come to the institution.

Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., said on Saturday that an arrest of Mr. Netanyahu “is not going to happen.” Responding to the mayor’s statement, he said the headquarters agreement grants diplomatic protections to visiting heads of government and that “federal authority trumps any local mayor’s wishes.”

Mr. Mamdani also responded on Monday to the brouhaha his statement about potentially arresting Mr. Netanyahu had made.

“When someone is charged with an international court warrant it’s something that should be taken seriously,” he said.

Representative Ro Khanna, Democrat of California, a vociferous critic of Israel and possible contender for president in 2028, told The Sunday Briefing on Fox News that he believed Mr. Netanyahu’s case should proceed in court, but that the U.N. should still welcome him at the world body.

“He can come to the U.N. Assembly,” Mr. Khanna said, adding, “I’m not for creating a spectacle. The U.N. is a place that people can come to.”

Sally Goldenberg contributed reporting.

item.title: Epidemics and Rage
item.description:
A few weeks ago, I spoke to my colleague Declan Walsh, who was reporting at the epicenter of the Ebola epidemic. One thing that stuck with me was the rage he described toward many of the health workers trying to contain the outbreak.

It reminded me of something I witnessed in Germany during Covid. There, too, anger was often directed at those whose goal was to help. There were weekly protests against restrictions, some of them violent. A gas station attendant was killed when he asked a man to wear a mask.

So what is it about health crises and rage? Today my colleague Sheri Fink explains why anger at health workers is something many societies have struggled with for centuries.

By Sheri Fink

Efforts to contain Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo did not begin well. Patients fled a treatment unit after community members set it on fire. Residents assaulted a burial team and forced the crew to turn over a coffin.

Reactions like this would be easy to chalk up to a poor understanding of how diseases spread. But unrest during epidemics is not about Ebola, Africa or education. It is something societies have struggled with for centuries, in rich countries and poor ones, in modern times and medieval ones. During the coronavirus pandemic, doctors, nurses and health officials around the world received not only applause and gratitude but also death threats. Patients denied that Covid existed even as they died of the disease.

Experts say outbreaks often elicit a contradictory mix of responses. First, people deny reality and put off behavioral changes that might slow the spread. Then they demand explanations, often blaming individuals, groups within society and, sometimes, doctors. Finally, people take action.

In the Democratic Republic of Congo, when armed community members remove a child from an Ebola treatment unit, “we may view that as irrational, illogical, kind of anti-science,” says Megan Schmidt-Sane, an American medical anthropologist who has briefed humanitarian groups fighting the current Ebola outbreak. “We know that this is about so much more than that. It’s about history and culture and politics and even just about how people love and care for others in their family who are sick.” Only when we understand these tendencies, she and other scholars say, can we navigate them.

Disease breeds distrust

Before the discovery that germs cause illness, humans searched for answers that might explain waves of disease and death. During the Black Death in the 14th century, Europeans massacred Jews, Catalans and others they accused of poisoning wells.

And even when scientific explanations came along, they still left people to fight over the science itself. Today, we can photograph the tiniest viruses and sequence their genetic codes, but considerable mystery and debate remain over how pathogens emerge, spread and kill.

Conspiracy theories about disease travel much more quickly now, but they have always been a part of outbreaks. Samuel Cohn, a professor of medieval history at the University of Glasgow, found that during cholera outbreaks in the 19th and 20th centuries, impoverished people in places as different as New York City and tsarist Russia “produced similar fantasies that accused elites of plotting to cull populations of the poor.” This mistrust led to the murder of medical professionals “and the ritualistic destruction of hospitals and medical equipment.” Sometimes the state is the party sowing blame. In the early 20th century, Ottomans accused Armenians of spreading typhus, and Nazis accused Jews of the same. And in recent years, conspiracy theories can travel the world faster than the disease itself.

There are some simple reasons people in the Democratic Republic of Congo are distrustful of hospitals in the current outbreak. The disease has no cure and acts very rapidly. Many patients have entered the hospital seeming not very sick but then quickly died, raising fears about sending relatives there.

But the Ebola outbreak is also just the latest shock after decades of conflict and suffering, state neglect, and colonial and postcolonial violence. Under Belgian colonial rule in the 20th century, officials confined people suspected of having sleeping sickness — a parasitic disease spread by tsetse flies — and experimented with toxic, arsenic-based treatments. Research suggests these types of efforts contributed to persistent medical distrust across multiple African countries.

“Both medicine and humanitarianism have been used” to advance outsiders’ interests, says Myfanwy James, a British assistant professor of international development at the London School of Economics and Political Science. “These deeply held suspicions actually are based on historical experience.”

Breaking through

In recent decades, anthropologists have tried to bridge the understanding between public health responders and the communities affected by deadly diseases. Many African countries now include anthropologists on outbreak response teams, says Julienne Anoko, a Cameroonian anthropologist who works on community engagement for the W.H.O.

Drawing on previous outbreaks, health workers in the Democratic Republic of Congo are now adapting burial practices to honor community beliefs while reducing the risk posed by infectious bodies. And after complaints, the entrance to an isolation unit was moved so that incoming patients do not have to walk past a morgue.

That work is painstaking; the results can be unsatisfying. And the broader challenge of containing the epidemic remains: Two months into the response, new Ebola cases are still growing faster than in any previous outbreak. More than half of those who contract the disease are dying without making contact with Ebola response teams.

But in places where health workers have been able to impart the true nature of the threat, more people are seeking help. They “accept the virus is killing them,” Anoko says, “and they are scared of dying.”

item.title: Britain’s New Leader Starts With Electricity Tax Cut
item.description:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain announced on Tuesday the elimination of value-added taxes on electricity, saying that the change would save households the equivalent of about $60 this year at a time of volatile energy costs.

The move, coming on Mr. Burnham’s second day in office, seemed intended to demonstrate his commitment to tackling high prices in Britain. That issue was central to the anger and frustration that many people cited when asked about Mr. Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, who announced his resignation last month.

In a statement, Mr. Burnham said that he wanted “to give people breathing space.”

“We’re taking immediate action to cut taxes on energy bills, put more money in people’s pockets and bring back hope,” he added.

Even as Mr. Burnham tries to address concerns about inflation, he is under pressure from the bond market not to add to Britain’s public debt. Political opponents have already accused him of wanting to raise taxes to pay for new government spending.

Aides said on Tuesday that the cut in electricity taxes would be paid for by scrapping Mr. Starmer’s plan to create a national digital ID card. They said the government would save about $2.4 billion by abandoning the idea, which was devised to curb illegal migration.

But Darren Jones, one of Mr. Starmer’s top allies who was fired from the cabinet by Mr. Burnham on Monday, wrote on social media on Tuesday that the digital ID program was “unfunded.”

“The government will have to set out how it will pay for its new policies at the budget,” he wrote.

Mr. Burnham’s announcement on electricity tax cuts came as he received a glowing initial assessment from President Trump in a late-night social media post, after the two leaders had a brief telephone conversation earlier in the day.

“The Prime Minister has got a big job ahead of him, but he will be able to do it and, of course, the U.S.A. will be there to help!” Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The call was interesting, and went very well. I wished Prime Minister Burnham, GOOD LUCK AND GODSPEED!”

Dealing with Mr. Trump and managing the relationship with the United States will be a key challenge for Mr. Burnham. In a recent interview, the British prime minister said that he would try to be himself when dealing with Mr. Trump and that he would meet the U.S. president “where he’s at.”

Mr. Burnham also made a flurry of appointments to his cabinet late into the night on Monday.

Wes Streeting, who had been the health secretary under Mr. Starmer and briefly considered challenging Mr. Burnham for the leadership of the Labour Party, will become defense secretary. Ed Miliband, former energy secretary, will lead the Foreign Office. Shabana Mahmood will stay as home secretary.

Perhaps the most surprising staffing move was Mr. Burnham’s decision to make John Healey, former defense secretary, the chancellor of the Exchequer, Britain’s top financial official.

Mr. Healey resigned from his defense post last month, telling Mr. Starmer in a resignation letter that Rachel Reeves, who was then the chancellor, was not spending enough money on the military. Now Mr. Healey has replaced Ms. Reeves and is in a position to change the direction of spending.

item.title: Lebanese Army Accuses Israeli Troops of Firing as Its Forces Deploy in ‘Pilot Zone’
item.description:
Israeli forces fired shots near Lebanese Army troops on Tuesday, both sides said, raising tensions as they took the first steps in a new U.S.-brokered plan to transfer control of occupied areas to Beirut after months of war.

There were no reported casualties in the gunfire, as Lebanese troops began deploying in a village in southern Lebanon after an Israeli withdrawal on Tuesday.

The incident occurred hours before President Joseph Aoun of Lebanon met with President Trump at the White House. The two leaders were expected to discuss the security situation in Lebanon, as well as efforts to secure Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory that it has occupied for months, since invading to battle Hezbollah.

The deployment was part of a phased arrangement under which Israel agreed to withdraw from areas in southern Lebanon while the Lebanese military moves in to secure them, allowing displaced residents to return. The areas, described as “pilot zones,” are meant to test a broader agreement reached last month between Lebanon and Israel to wind down the conflict.

The Lebanese Army said in a statement on Tuesday that it had begun deploying to the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiya in the southern Nabatieh district. The army urged residents not to return until the security situation had stabilized and asked them to follow the instructions of troops on the ground.

Hours later, the Lebanese military accused Israeli forces of opening fire near their units. In a statement, they added that “this act of aggression could hinder the implementation of deployment steps in the pilot areas.”

The Israeli military said in a statement that Lebanese forces entered an area outside of the designated “pilot zone.” Israeli soldiers “operating in the area fired warning shots into the air only, which did not endanger the Lebanese Armed Forces personnel, in order to distance them from the area.”

In Lebanon, critics of the deal say it has not set a firm timetable for Israel’s withdrawal, which is tied to the Lebanese government’s efforts to disarm Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group that the government does not control. Hezbollah was not party to the negotiations with Israel and has rejected the framework agreement.

Israel’s military said late on Monday that Israeli, American and Lebanese military teams were conducting joint planning and coordination to implement the agreement. As part of the deal reached last month, Israel and Lebanon also agreed to establish a military coordination group overseen by the United States.

The State Department said in a statement on Monday that the initial “pilot zone” operations would include the villages of Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiya. Israel and Lebanon have held rare diplomatic talks for months, meeting first in Washington and then in Rome.

Hezbollah has rejected the negotiations with Israel, as well as efforts by the Lebanese government to disarm the group, adding to uncertainty about the broader agreement, how it can be carried out and Lebanon’s fragile path toward stability.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday, Mr. Trump and Mr. Aoun said they would discuss ways to support the Lebanese Army and help stabilize Lebanon, which has faced severe political and economic crises in recent years. Asked whether he would speak to Hezbollah, Mr. Trump said he would, particularly if Mr. Aoun wanted him to.

“I would speak to Hezbollah,” he said. “I speak to everybody. I will speak to people that a lot of people think I shouldn’t be speaking to and things work out.”

On Tuesday, some analysts said that the Israeli withdrawal, though limited in scope, could offer the Lebanese government an opportunity to bolster its standing.

“Withdrawing from the area does not make a massive difference on the ground,” said David Wood, the senior Lebanon analyst at the International Crisis Group, a research organization. “But the Lebanese state will hope that it can use this first ‘pilot zone’ as a proof of concept, showing that the Lebanese Army can assert control effectively, and therefore the U.S. should push Israel to accept further ‘pilot zones’ in fully occupied areas of Lebanese territory.”

The latest round of fighting erupted in early March after Hezbollah attacked Israel in response to the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran that began in late February. More than 4,300 people have been killed in Lebanon and over 12,000 wounded in the latest conflict, according to Lebanese health officials. Israeli officials say at least four Israeli civilians and more than 30 soldiers have been killed.

By Tuesday afternoon, footage on social media and local television showed residents of the Zawtar al-Gharbiya, along with ambulances, attempting to access the area. But Abed Ezzedine, the village’s mayor, said that Lebanese troops had told residents they would not be able to access the town on Tuesday.

“The Lebanese Army is doing its best to clear the roads and streets within the town,” Mr. Ezzedine said in a phone interview. “I am anxiously waiting with other people to get into the town. I can’t wait to see Zawtar again.”

Hwaida Saad and Leo Sands contributed reporting.

item.title: 1,700 H.I.V. Treatment Sites Closed After Trump Aid Cuts, a Study Finds
item.description:
The Trump administration’s cuts to the largest global H.I.V. program last year resulted in sharp drops in both prevention efforts and treatment for the people most at risk from the disease, according to the first large survey of organizations that had received the funds.

The findings show a grimmer picture of the impact of the cuts than the State Department’s data, released in April, which seemed to suggest that the program had helped to treat about as many people last year as it had in 2024.

To comply with the administration’s policies, the new survey, conducted by the H.I.V. charity amfAR, found, three-quarters of the organizations stopped providing services to those at highest risk from H.I.V. — sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people and people who inject drugs. The results are scheduled to be presented next week at a large international AIDS conference in Rio de Janeiro.

A second study, conducted by a multinational group of scientists, which will also be presented at the conference, found that the cuts had disproportionately affected children with H.I.V. The program, called the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR, supported treatment for about 77,000 fewer children in 2025 than it had the previous year, representing a 14 percent decline, the study found.

“We have not verified this specific report, but we can categorically say that its methodology is flawed,” the State Department, which oversees PEPFAR, said in an emailed statement. “The Trump Administration has strengthened PEPFAR through clear strategic direction, promoting greater recipient-country ownership, and sharpening the program’s focus on measurable health outcomes.”

Worldwide, nearly half of all children living with H.I.V. do not have access to treatment, according to UNAIDS, the United Nations program.

President George W. Bush started PEPFAR in January 2003, when H.I.V. medications were still unavailable in many parts of the world. The program is credited with saving 26 million lives, across more than 50 countries, making it the most successful endeavor of its kind.

But last year the Trump administration reshaped the program, saying the low-income nations that benefited must take on more of the costs of treating and preventing H.I.V. among their own citizens.

“We unfortunately are going through a very complex and difficult moment, where all these good achievements are challenged by the new policies,” Dr. Beatriz Grinsztejn, president of the International AIDS Society, said at a press briefing last week.

It is too early to gauge the impact of the cuts on H.I.V. rates, and it may continue to be challenging because many data collection programs have been scaled back or shut down as a result of the U.S. aid cuts.

In the first study, researchers collected information from 166 organizations, about one-quarter of the total funded by PEPFAR, in 46 countries. Delayed or terminated awards in 2025 caused these groups to shut down at least 1,700 sites that had delivered H.I.V. services, and to lay off more than 16,000 workers, the survey found.

Just six organizations accounted for 85 percent of the site closures, an indication of how the loss of funding to a single recipient can shutter hundreds of service points at once, the researchers said.

Sites that stayed open also felt the effects of the cuts.

“Even if a site doesn’t close, what you’re seeing is longer wait times, and fewer staff, and nonfunctioning data systems,” said Jennifer Sherwood, amfAR’s director of research and public policy.

The disruptions hit local organizations the hardest, contrary to the administration’s stated goal of empowering such groups and helping them move away from multinational aid organizations, she said.

After an initial freeze on all PEPFAR funds early in 2025, the administration allowed treatment to continue, but limited funds for prevention mostly to programs to stop transmission of H.I.V. from pregnant and breastfeeding women to their children.

In January, the administration also expanded the so-called Mexico City Policy, forbidding organizations that receive U.S. funds from providing most services related to gender, diversity, and reproductive health. More than 60 percent of organizations stopped providing at least one service and 44 percent stopped serving specific populations, the amfAR survey found.

Some organizations were required to revise their materials and strip out words that pertained to specific topics, and some of those changes altered the larger meaning. For example, in one case, “sex work” was revised to read “sex trafficking,” a term “which describes something entirely different,” noted Elise Lankiewicz, a policy associate at amfAR.

In some cases, the changes had nothing at all to do with prohibited concepts, and flagged phrases like “transfer of knowledge,” perhaps because it contained the fragment “trans.”

About half of the organizations surveyed also reported disruptions in their supply chains, including difficulty procuring condoms, lab supplies and antiretroviral drugs for treatment.

“For better or worse, PEPFAR ended up being a really interconnected system,” Ms. Lankiewicz said. “Trying to carve out and cancel certain awards had ripple impacts throughout the whole program.”

The system that is left “is really a treatment-heavy model, which isn’t really conducive to controlling the H.I.V. epidemic long-term,” she added.

But some evidence suggests the cuts have also affected treatment. In a separate analysis published last month in the journal Nature Health, Ramona Godbole, a senior manager at the Clinton Health Access Initiative, and other researchers reported a 10 percent decrease in the number of people treated with support from PEPFAR.

In the new study to be presented next week, the same researchers focused on PEPFAR support for children living with H.I.V., because they “can get very sick very quickly without access to drugs, and so the stakes are really high,” Ms. Godbole said.

The State Department said its policies have reduced the number of children becoming infected in the first place. “The number of children testing positive and on treatment for H.I.V. has continued to decline,” the department said in its statement.

The number of children receiving treatment for H.I.V. has slowly been decreasing in recent years because of the success of efforts to prevent babies from being born with the virus. But the 14.2 percent decline last year was a bigger drop than has been seen before, she said. India and South Africa each reported a decline of more than 45 percent.

“It’s a signal, not a verdict,” Ms. Godbole said. “But it’s certainly the signal to do more investigation.”

item.title: Water Plants Under Fire in the Gulf Are Crucial to Civilians
item.description:
The resurgence in hostilities between the United States and Iran has put desalination plants under renewed threat across the Persian Gulf region, where tens of millions of people rely on such facilities for drinking water.

In recent days, Kuwait has accused Iran of striking energy and water plants, igniting fires that have forced officials to suspend operations at several facilities. Earlier in the war, officials in Bahrain and Iran said desalination plants in those countries had also come under fire.

Infrastructure that civilians rely on for survival is not generally considered a legitimate military target, and striking it could be considered a war crime. But the attacks on water resources are especially concerning in the Gulf region: Most nations there lack widespread access to fresh water and rely heavily on hundreds of desalination plants, complex operations where repairs can be difficult and time-consuming.

Desalination plants produce 90 percent of Kuwait’s drinking water, according to an analysis by the French Institute of International Relations. Oman (86 percent) and Saudi Arabia (70 percent) also rely heavily on the technology.

Such plants have proliferated in the region as climate change has made droughts more frequent and severe, and as desalination technology has improved. The plants either evaporate and condense salt water or filter it through fine membranes.

Iran does not lean as heavily on desalination plants as its neighbors, but has faced severe water shortages in recent years. Iran has accused U.S. strikes of disabling water infrastructure in locations including an island where officials say water access for 30 villages was affected. The Pentagon and Israel denied responsibility for those attacks.

Iran and the United States have accused each other of targeting sensitive infrastructure during the latest exchanges of attacks, and Iran has said it would respond to any U.S. attacks on its own infrastructure by hitting similar targets in nearby countries that are allied with the United States.

That has prompted calls from around the globe for vital infrastructure to be spared from attacks.

“As in any conflict, the protection of civilians and civilian objects is critical,” said Stéphane Dujarric, a spokesman for the United Nations secretary-general, speaking about the conflict in a briefing on Monday. “Vital infrastructure on which civilians rely for survival, including hospitals and water supplies, must be spared.”

item.title: What to Know About Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain
item.description:
President Trump on Tuesday reiterated his threat to bomb a suspected Iranian nuclear site known as Pickaxe Mountain, telling reporters that the United States would strike that area “pretty soon, and very heavily.”

“There’s not a thing they can do about it,” he said of the Iranians during an Oval Office meeting with President Joseph Aoun of Lebanon. “Normally I wouldn’t say that. If I thought they could do something about it, I would never say that.”

Little has been confirmed about Pickaxe Mountain beyond its existence. When Mr. Trump threatened to bomb the site earlier this month, he acknowledged that “we see no activity there” but that it was still a “possible target for a nice big fat shot right in their front door.”

Here’s what to know about Pickaxe Mountain.

Pickaxe Mountain is in central Iran, about one mile away from the Natanz uranium enrichment facility, which was bombed by the United States and Israel in March, during the current war, as well as during the June 2025 war. The mountain is known locally as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La.

According to the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, the mountain itself rises nearly 5,300 feet above sea level, and the facility is estimated to be buried more than 300 feet below it.

Experts say the site has been under construction since 2020 and is not yet operational. Satellite imagery shows that construction continued after the June 2025 bombings and that a security wall was recently built around the facility’s perimeter. Some entrances were also reinforced — possibly to protect against future attacks.

Iranian officials said in 2020 that Pickaxe Mountain would hold a plant to build centrifuges, after one at Natanz was destroyed earlier that year in what Iran deemed an act of Israeli sabotage. Centrifuges are machines that spin uranium at supersonic speeds to enrich it and produce nuclear fuel. The uranium would need to be enriched further, with many more steps taken, in order to build a nuclear weapon.

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful, but it has not allowed the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, to gain access to Pickaxe Mountain. Rafael Grossi, the director general of the I.A.E.A., told reporters early last year that he had repeatedly pressed Iran for more information about the site at Pickaxe Mountain but to no avail.

“We’re asking them, ‘What is this for?’” Mr. Grossi said. “They are telling us, ‘It’s none of your business.’”

The site at Pickaxe Mountain is buried so deep that experts say even the United States’ most powerful bunker-busting bombs, like the 30,000-pound bombs that blasted through Iran’s mountainside uranium enrichment facility at Fordo and disabled its centrifuges in June 2025, might not be effective.

The site at Pickaxe Mountain may still have weaknesses that could make it vulnerable to aerial attacks, but it “would be more suitable for ground forces to attack or sabotage,” the Institute for Science and International Security has said. Still, since the U.S. military would need to fly deep into central Iran to reach Pickaxe Mountain, troops could be left exposed to ground fire on their way in and to drone and missile attacks once on the ground.

item.title: A Wartime Rift in Ukraine
item.description:
For a while now, there has been a sense that the tide has turned for Ukraine in its war with Russia. Ukraine is attacking Moscow; it’s even getting praise from President Trump. So why did President Volodymyr Zelensky just fire his top general?

War can be uniquely challenging for democracies, where citizens expect to have a say and sometimes express their discontent on the streets. Today my colleague Andrew Kramer writes about the upheaval in Kyiv during what should be a moment of optimism. It’s a fight over drones, corruption, generational differences and more.

By Andrew E. Kramer

For a time, it looked like Ukraine was going to have a good summer.

After a winter of heavy Russian bombardment, the country was finding battlefield success, striking Moscow and hitting Russian ships in the Black and Azov Seas. It was finding diplomatic success, too, receiving billions of euros from the European Union and a promise from Trump that Ukraine could start manufacturing its own interceptor missiles. Ukraine was on a winning streak.

What snapped it was not a fearsome Russian offensive or another unraveling of relations with Trump. Instead, it was an outbreak of political infighting at home.

The defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, was openly clashing with Oleksandr Syrskyi, the country’s top general. Zelensky fired Fedorov last week, triggering major street protests. He then fired Syrskyi on Tuesday night.

(You can read more about the breaking story of the general’s dismissal here.)

The infighting has cracked the all-important sense of wartime unity and overshadowed the narrative that Ukraine is riding high in the war. Rather than capitalizing on its momentum, Ukraine is now grappling with military upheaval at a critical juncture — a reminder that being a democracy at war can be messy.

A generation gap

The rift has raised questions about how fully Ukraine, with its vaunted reputation for military innovation, is embracing the high-tech solutions that the popular, youthful Fedorov embodied.

During his tenure, Fedorov, 35, clashed with Ukraine’s generals, who saw aspects of his robot-war vision as fanciful and argued for the continued need for infantry deployments.

Fedorov was ultimately fired after he blocked purchases of artillery ammunition in favor of drones. Syrskyi insisted that the ammunition was still needed in the brutal trench fighting in the country’s east.

But Fedorov didn’t back down. Instead, he responded with a press conference, where he delivered the most scathing public critique of Ukraine’s military leadership so far during the war.

Fedorov accused the 60-year-old Syrskyi, an old-school general, of strategic shortsightedness — of thwarting the careers of promising junior commanders and resisting the drone and robot combat that’s transforming the war. He said he had sought to root out what he described as rampant corruption in defense procurement and made enemies as a result.

In the aftermath of his firing, protesters poured out into cities across the country, many of them carrying signs with variations on “Fedorov is innovation, old grandpas are degeneration.”

In the days since, however, what began as a show of support for Fedorov morphed into demands for Zelensky to fire Syrskyi.

Crowds in Kyiv, which included active-duty soldiers and veterans, began deriding the man who successfully commanded pivotal battles earlier in the war. Meanwhile, a cardboard cutout of Fedorov got cheers when it appeared on a balcony overlooking the demonstration.

Ukrainian leaders take street protests seriously. They’ve toppled multiple governments. They’re viewed as a pillar of democracy and as an important contrast to the authoritarianism of Russia under President Vladimir Putin.

It wasn’t long before Zelensky was holding back-to-back video calls with army commanders, showing a willingness to hear their complaints. By Tuesday evening, Syrskyi was gone.

When success breeds pushback

One Ukrainian journalist told me that the rift over how to wage the war had come into the open now “precisely because there are successes” on the battlefield.

The people advocating high-tech warfare felt vindicated and became more vocal, said Volodymyr Yermolenko, the editor of a culture and politics magazine. Then those favoring a more conventional approach pushed back.

But that sort of clash carries risks. “Ukrainian history shows that if we are united, it’s very difficult to win against Ukraine,” Yermolenko said.

“The biggest enemy is internal division,” he said. “Our history taught us this can be deadly.”

Will these firings be enough to restore unity?

item.title: Philippines Says Sailor Was Injured in Skirmish With Chinese Coast Guard
item.description:
The Philippine military accused China’s coast guard of injuring one of its sailors in a scuffle that broke out on Monday in the South China Sea, where the two countries have been locked in a decades-long territorial dispute.

The episode began when an inflatable Chinese coast guard boat approached the Sierra Madre, a beached World War II-era warship that the Philippines uses as a military outpost in a disputed reef, and lashed out at the Philippine sailors who approached in a boat to chase them away, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said in a statement.

The statement added that a Philippine sailor had been struck on the head with a wooden baton in the ensuing struggle, necessitating medical care.

The Philippines’ Department of National Defense decried the incident as another act of “harassment” by the Chinese coast guard that added to a “pattern of provocative and hostile behavior,” in a statement of Monday. “We simply cannot trust this belligerent neighbor.”

The Chinese coast guard has disputed that version of events, saying that the Philippine sailors rammed their patrol boat first before attacking its personnel with “oars, long sticks, and other tools.”

Accusing the Philippines of spreading propaganda, China’s foreign ministry said it had summoned the Philippine ambassador in Beijing over the incident, according to a statement published by state media on Tuesday. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines has done the same to China’s ambassador in Manila.

While several countries have longstanding territorial claims in the South China Sea, the dispute between China and the Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally, has been the most fraught.

Tensions in the region have steadily increased in recent years, with the Philippines denouncing the encroachment of Chinese vessels, which they say have used water cannons or lasers to harass Philippine sailors in the area. In another incident at the Second Thomas Shoal — where the Sierra Madre is beached — in 2024, a Filipino soldier lost a finger after a Chinese boat rammed his vessel.

The latest flare-up came just before the start of a series of high-level diplomatic meetings hosted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, where, among other agenda items like the wars in Myanmar and Iran, negotiations to ease tensions in the South China Sea are expected to continue. The gathering, which will conclude Thursday, is being attended by both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and China’s foreign minister, Wang Yi.

The Philippines, the current chair of the 11-member ASEAN, has made establishing a legally binding code of conduct to prevent escalations in the South China Sea a key priority for its tenure, which concludes at the end of this year. The code was proposed decades ago and Philippine officials have voiced optimism about recent progress. But intractable differences have loomed.

Chief among them is the landmark ruling by an international tribunal that dismissed most of China’s sweeping territorial claims in the South China Sea in 2016, including those on the area marked by the Sierra Madre. While there was no mechanism for enforcing the ruling, it was widely regarded as a major victory for the Philippines, which currently sees it as a legal base line for any maritime code of conduct. China, which refused to participate in the arbitration, has steadfastly rejected it.

The decision provided fodder for another dispute earlier this month, when, in response to the Philippines’ commemoration of its 10th anniversary, Chinese state media posted a video depicting the Philippines as a monkey doing the bidding of Japan and the United States.

While the United States does not have any territorial claims of its own in the South China Sea, it conducts regular joint military drills there with the Philippines, with which it has a mutual defense treaty. Beijing has denounced U.S. involvement as a major source of tensions in the region.

The U.S. State Department criticized what it called “dangerous and aggressive actions” by China in a statement on the incident on Monday.

In an opinion article published by Philippine media outlets ahead of the ASEAN meeting, Mr. Rubio reiterated U.S. support for the 2016 ruling, writing that “we will honor our obligations to the Philippines and other allies as they confront new and coercive threats to our shared interests.” But he stopped short of singling out China by name.

Jason Gutierrez contributed reporting from Manila. Ruoxin Zhang contributed research.

item.title: A Family’s Daring Escape From North Korea ‘to Live and Stand Tall’
item.description:
Rain lashed a flimsy wooden boat as it tossed through a churning sea, its engine straining against the swell. Under the cover of a stormy night three years ago, the vessel was fleeing North Korea.

On board were nine people, including two small children and a woman who was six months pregnant. Only a couple of the passengers had seafaring experience. They eluded a patrol ship, speeding across the world’s most heavily guarded maritime border.

Soon after their boat lurched into South Korean waters, a high-speed warship of the South’s navy bore down on it, tearing the water in aggressive circles. Snipers on the vessel trained their laser sights on the chests of the three adult men on the wooden boat.

Through a loudspeaker, a voice boomed: “Are you lost? Engine trouble?”

The North Koreans shouted: “Please help. We are defecting.”

The red dots remained stubbornly fixed on their chests. The South Koreans were taking no chances: The three men were clad in North Korean military uniforms, camouflage for a high-stakes escape. Desperate, the men shouted into the boat’s cramped hold for the other passengers to emerge in order to prove that they were civilians. From below, the two children, a 5-year-old girl and 3-year-old boy, were hauled up first, both pale and wasted from seasickness. Only then did the red dots drop off.

The North Koreans, led by Kim Il-hyeok and his younger brother, Yi-hyeok, were bound together by blood and marriage. The brothers, both in their 30s at the time, were accompanied by their mother and their families: Il-heyok’s partner, who was pregnant, and Yi-hyeok’s wife, their two children, his mother-in-law and brother-in-law.

The family, who defected in 2023, were among the few who managed to escape North Korea after its leader, Kim Jong-un, imposed a crushing lockdown during the coronavirus pandemic. They arrived in their adopted country with rare insights into a nation that had been choked off from the outside world. Some details of their escape have not been previously reported.

“That night,” said Yi-hyeok’s wife, Yu-mi, “we crossed from a sea of darkness to a sea of freedom.”

Over several months of interviews in South Korea, Il-hyeok ​spoke with the same swagger that he had developed as a self-described “troublemaker” in North Korea. Yu-mi ​was reserved, pulling her legs tightly to her chest as she spoke. Her mother, who asked not to be named but agreed to be photographed, weighed every word, fearing how her comments might affect relatives left behind in the North. But they all spoke with conviction about why they had to leave North Korea. (The rest of the extended family declined to be interviewed.)

The brothers came from Pyoksong, a county in North Korea’s southwest.

During the famine of the late 1990s, their father, a railway security official, returned with grim accounts from the hardest-hit provinces: The emaciated bodies of children found outside train stations were frozen solid, thumping like frozen fish when they were tossed onto trucks headed to burial grounds. He was the first in the family to lose faith in a ruling class that was unable to feed its people.

One night after his sons reached adulthood, he took them to a hill and pointed toward a cluster of lights across the South Korean border.

“That’s where we should go,” he said. “To live and stand tall.”

Yu-mi lived in the ​nearby coastal town of Kangryong. From there, she could see planes glinting in the sun as they rose from Incheon International Airport, just across the water — a shimmering vision of possibility, yet unreachable for North Koreans barred from travel and cut off from the internet.

“Our country felt like a prison without bars,” she said.

Beginning in kindergarten, children sang the anthem “We Have Nothing to Envy,” even as they were mobilized to haul river water or scour hills for herbs and pine nuts.​ After long workdays, adults attended compulsory “life review sessions,” writing self-criticism and pledges of loyalty. When Kim Jong-un visited ​an island near Yu-mi’s town in 2013, soldiers and villagers swarmed into the sea in jubilation. She knew the scene was staged; ordinary residents, she said, had been banned from leaving home.

In the face of the propaganda, a contraband culture spread. South Korean films and dramas circulated on USB drives smuggled from China. In Kangryong, the devices also arrived inside plastic bottles released by South Korean activists across the water, along with rice and mini-Bibles. Officials warned the bottles contained poison, but South Korean entertainment was winning.

Il-hyeok idolized K-pop groups like Girls’ Generation and styled his hair in a mohawk like BigBang’s Taeyang. He was arrested for “capitalist delinquency” and released only after paying a bribe, his hair razored. He and his friends once secretly watched “Valkyrie,” the Tom Cruise film about the plot to kill Hitler. When the conspirators failed and were executed, his friends wept.

The brothers’ notion of deserting North Korea felt just as perilous. Their father forbade them from marrying, reasoning that the larger the family, the greater the risk of being caught while defecting. He then used connections to transfer Yi-hyeok, his youngest, to Kangryong, where he learned navigation, mapped guard posts, and cultivated ties with officials. Yi-hyeok became a helmet diver, who harvests seafood from the ocean floor, breathing fresh air piped through a surface hose. He eventually met Yu-mi.

Il-hyeok worked in North Korea’s shadow economy, bribing his way into opportunity and out of trouble. He butchered animals for restaurants, ran a small gold mine and bought rice stolen from state granaries, reselling it at a profit. He also grew disillusioned with the system he was gaming.

Then, in 2014, their father died unexpectedly. The South Korean dream seemed to die with him.

Where Il-hyeok, the older brother, was restless, Yi-hyeok was steady. He married Yu-mi in 2017, and the couple soon had their two children. He joined a military-run fisheries company, operating three vessels. Despite a United Nations ban, Chinese buyers worked openly in Kangryong, and on a good day Yi-hyeok could earn more than a typical worker​’s annual salary.

Il-hyeok began dating a kindergarten teacher. Defection was no longer a priority.

“When I mentioned it, my brother told me to watch my mouth,” Il-hyeok recalled.

The pandemic overturned everything.

North Korea imposed one of the world’s harshest lockdowns. In Kangryong, access to the sea was closed off with barbed wire and armed guards. Yi-hyeok’s boats rusted and his debts mounted. Officials claimed that South Korea was dumping infected bodies and waste into border waters. Yet boats supplying seafood to the top tiers of society continued to fish.

“The elites still ate whatever they wanted,” Yu-mi said.

Il-hyeok​ once filmed a gaunt toothless man in rags begging for food. The man said soldiers had shot a villager who tried to gather crabs.

“They are ruthless,” he said in a tired whisper. “Even if you won’t give alms, you shouldn’t break the beggar’s bowl.”

Public executions grew more frequent, targeting those accused of committing violent crimes like murder, which surged during the lockdown, or of distributing “nonsocialist” content such as South Korean dramas. Thousands, including the brothers, were forced to watch as rifle fire cracked across the execution grounds. The crowds dispersed in silence.

“The goal was to instill fear,” Il-hyeok said. “To erase any fantasy about the outside world.”

The authorities were closing in on him, too.

​He wanted to marry his girlfriend, the daughter of a farmer. In a system that claimed to be classless, marrying a woman who worked on a collective farm — even as a teacher — would mean a loss of status for Il-hyeok. Both families opposed the match. The couple moved in together anyway. Then, in 2022, Kim Jong‑un banned unmarried cohabitation. Offenders faced labor camps.

“I had to choose between her and North Korea,” Il-hyeok said. “I chose South Korea — and a true class revolution.”

The brothers no longer argued about whether to leave — only how.

By early 2023, North Korea had begun easing its pandemic restrictions. Yi-hyeok’s boats were among the first permitted back to sea. But the window to escape was already closing. The authorities were preparing to install surveillance cameras along the coast to deter defections.

The brothers spoke in code over the phone. “Good weather” meant a storm was coming, forcing patrol boats back to port. “We’ve got a good catch — come down here” meant Il-hyeok should bring their mother and his girlfriend to Kangryong.

The weather and the catch were ideal the night of May 6, 2023.

Yu-mi’s mot​her, a 52-year-old widow, signed up last, just five hours before departure.

“I could die trying to escape,” she said. “But if my family reached the South and I stayed behind, I’d be as good as dead anyway — the relative of traitors.”

Yi-hyeok’s brother-in-law, his fishing partner, slipped away by boat and waited offshore. The rest of the family crossed a coastal hill strewn with land mines to reach a secluded beach. To carry Yi-hyeok’s two young children more easily, the brothers sealed them inside burlap sacks and hoisted them onto their shoulders. Before they closed the sacks, Yu-mi caught her children looking up at her.

“I thought it might be the last time I’d ever see them,” she said. “I cried, and my husband teared up, too.”

Yi-hyeok’s brother-in-law spotted the prearranged signal — a flashlight blinking three times from the beach — and steered the boat in to pick up the rest of the extended family. Around 10 p.m., the 30-foot-long vessel pulled away, its engine throttled down to little more than a brisk walking pace as it tried to slip quietly toward Yeonpyeong Island in South Korea, just nine miles away.

Below deck, Yu-mi suddenly felt ​the engine roar to full throttle, filling the hold with black exhaust and leaving the women and children seasick. Her youngest child’s eyes rolled back. She carried him up for fresh air — and found the men on deck in a panic.

“That’s when I saw a searchlight from a North Korean patrol boat sweeping across the waves behind us,” she said. “My heart dropped.”

The brothers had already agreed on what to do if they couldn’t outrun a security vessel: strap life jackets and flashlights onto the women and children and send them into the sea, trusting the current to carry them south. The men would steer the boat away as a decoy, making a last stand with 20-inch knives and homemade red-pepper bombs. To lighten the boat, Il-hyeok threw anything heavy overboard — axes, wrenches, fishing net, his brother’s air compressor for helmet diving.

​He ran below deck, fastened a life jacket onto his partner and rushed back outside. She believed he was about to throw her into the sea to save the others. His mother​ thought her son had chosen to save his girlfriend before his mother.

“It gave me endless trouble with them, until I could convince them they’d misunderstood me,” he said.

Gradually, the searchlight behind them faded. The brothers later speculated that the fishing net they had thrown overboard had tangled in the pursuing boat’s propeller.

Their two-hour gamble ended shortly after midnight, after the South Korean vessel stopped them and all nine family members were brought aboard.

An officer greeted them: “Welcome to paradise.”

Before the​y disembarked, the officer raised his fist and shouted, “Fighting!” The English word — common in South Korea as encouragement — was unfamiliar to the North Koreans.

“But he was smiling and shaking our hands,” Yu-mi said, “so we assumed he wished us well.”

​In the South, Yu-mi studied to gain an accounting clerk certificate and found work at a school. Her brother enrolled in college, while Yi-hyeok returned to helmet-diving for seafood.

“My brother joked the diving gear here was so advanced he could fall asleep underwater if he wanted to,” Il-hyeok recalled.

Il-hyeok’s girlfriend gave birth to their first child in the South. The couple married in 2024 and soon welcomed another daughter. Il-hyeok is finding his footing in the South’s capitalist economy, trying part-time jobs at restaurants and operating forklifts and excavators.

The plunge into the South’s noisy democracy was overwhelming. Televisions offered endless channels — so different from the North, where only government broadcasts existed. Back home, Il-hyeok’s ​used motorbike was a prized status symbol​; now he found himself on highways crowded with modern cars. City squares rang with protests.

Yu-mi’s mother marveled at faucets that produced both hot and cold water. On her first day working at a nursing home, ​she faltered when colleagues asked for “napkins” — another English word she had never heard. The brothers’ mother was scandalized by a TV drama in which a wife slapped her husband. And when Il-hyeok first ventured beyond Seoul, the South’s capital, he dutifully called a police detective to ask for permission. The detective only laughed.

And then there were elections.

In the North, ​people lined up in formal dress to receive a ballot with only one name. ​They placed ​their vote in the “yes” box with both hands and bowed deeply to portraits of Kim Jong-un’s father and grandfather, who ruled before him. No one dared approach the “no” box.​ When Il-hyeok and his wife voted in June as South Korean citizens, they found voters arriving in shorts and slippers, earphones in place. The ballot was a bewildering list of names.

Yet, South Korea was no paradise.

After 19 months in the South, Yi-hyeok died in a diving accident in late 2024.​ The brothers’ mother and Il-hyeok’s wife were diagnosed with cancer.

Il-hyeok vented frustration at Seoul’s soaring housing prices. He is saving every penny to move his family out of their cramped, government-subsidized rental apartment. Still, he insisted the defection was “100 percent” the right choice.​ Before his death, Yi-hyeok appeared on television, explaining that he fled to spare his children the indoctrination of North Korean schools. His daughter is now a second grader at a South Korean school, and his son is in kindergarten. The children adapted fastest to their new lives, quickly embracing South Korean staples like fried chicken and pizza.

“My husband gave me and our children the freedom he promised before he died,” Yu-mi said.

The brothers also honored their father’s final wish: When their boat fled North Korea, they carried his ashes with them.

I’ve been captivated by the recent defection of nine North Koreans to South Korea. It is exceedingly rare for an entire extended family to escape together, especially across the heavily guarded maritime border dividing the two Koreas. As it turns out, their escape plan was actually years in the making. I’ve pieced their journey together — a tale of brutal hardships during the pandemic era and a daring search for freedom.

@Choe Sang-Hun This is a beautiful story -- of desperation, great courage, of the bitter-sweetness of "paradise." It also reminded me -- as it should all those who enjoy the luxury of freedom -- of my good fortune. Thanks for sharing this family's journey with NYT readers.
